analysis.one_liner: Bans banks from charging surcharges to non-customers using their ATMs.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which held two hearings but never acted before the Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend a 1978 consumer law, the Electronic Fund Transfer Act, to bar banks and other ATM owners from charging a surcharge to someone using their machine who does not bank with them. When you withdraw cash from another bank's ATM today, that machine's owner can add a fee on top of whatever your own bank charges; this bill would outlaw that second, machine-owner fee. It would not stop banks from charging their own customers for using other banks' machines.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who withdraw cash from a bank where they hold no account. The bill would prohibit the surcharge that the owner or operator of an ATM imposes on such transactions when they run through a national or regional banking network, eliminating a fee that can be charged several times a month by someone who needs cash away from home.

how_it_helps.text: Defines an 'electronic terminal surcharge' as the fee assessed by the financial institution that owns or operates the ATM.

Prohibits that surcharge whenever the transaction does not involve an account at the machine's owner and is conducted through a national or regional electronic banking network — in practice, nearly every out-of-network ATM withdrawal.
Adds this limit to the Electronic Fund Transfer Act, the federal consumer law that already governs debit-card and ATM transactions.

analysis.who_pays: Banks and other ATM owners, which lose the per-use surcharge revenue they collect from non-customers — a fee stream that grew quickly in the mid-1990s after the national ATM networks stopped banning it.

drawbacks.text: Removing the surcharge takes away revenue that machine owners said covered the cost of installing and operating ATMs in convenience stores, gas stations, and other off-premise locations; critics argued a ban could lead banks to remove machines from low-traffic places.

The bill targets only the fee charged by the ATM's owner. A consumer's own bank could still charge a fee for using another bank's machine, so out-of-network withdrawals would not necessarily become free.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers the benefit is direct and easy to see: the extra fee for using someone else's machine disappears. The cost falls on banks, which argued the fees paid for keeping machines in far-flung locations; the honest tradeoff is possible fewer ATMs in remote or low-volume spots against lower fees everywhere else. The bill also left one fee untouched — what your own bank charges you — so relief would have been partial.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which held hearings on it twice but never reported it or brought it to a vote, and it died when the Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Sen. Alfonse D'Amato introduced the Fair ATM Fees for Consumers Act on June 11, 1997, joined by original cosponsors including Democrats John Kerry, Barbara Boxer, Carol Moseley-Braun, and Patty Murray and Republican Lincoln Chafee.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
The Banking Committee held hearings on the bill on June 11, 1997 and again on July 29, 1997.
Eleven senators cosponsored the bill — nine Democrats and two Republicans.

The sponsor gave introductory remarks again on April 1, 1998, but no further action followed; the bill never reached a committee vote or the Senate floor, and the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and ATM owners kept the surcharge revenue the bill would have taken away. Consumers continued paying the machine-owner fee on out-of-network withdrawals, and the issue resurfaced in later Congresses without result here.

for.name: Sen. Alfonse D'Amato
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, gave introductory remarks on the floor twice, and as chair of the Banking Committee held hearings on it.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Kerry, Boxer, Bryan, Moseley-Braun, and Murray among the original cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Banking Committee
against.what_they_did: Held hearings twice but never reported the bill or scheduled a vote, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Banking industry
against.what_they_did: Banks argued surcharges fund the cost of deploying ATMs and opposed legislative bans on the fees during this period.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was bipartisan but small: a Republican sponsor, nine of 45 Senate Democrats and two of 55 Senate Republicans cosponsoring, with no roll-call votes ever taken to show a broader split.

industries.note: The bill would prohibit the surcharge ATM owners charge non-customers for each withdrawal, cutting off a growing fee stream. The industry's interest in keeping the fee ran directly against consumers' interest in cheaper cash access.

Non-bank operators of machines in stores and other locations collect the same owner surcharge on non-customer transactions; the ban would remove that revenue, which they said offset the cost of operating machines outside bank branches.

The bill applies to transactions run through national or regional electronic banking networks; a surcharge ban could change the fee economics that drew banks into these networks, though it would not ban the networks themselves.
